text:
Vestact Articles (34) My Homepage Follow For many of us, yesterday was the first day of back to work, back to reality. In this day and age it is quite easy to stay online and in touch remotely. Watching the markets day by day over the festive season was not very festive at all. The US market had one of its worst Christmas periods ever. Instead of a Santa Rally, we got a Santa Flop. Having said all that, since Christmas eve the S&P 500 has recovered by 8.5%. So maybe Santa was just a little delayed this year. Let's blame it on the weather.
In all seriousness, there are a few things raising market anxiety levels at the moment. Of course, Donald Trump's trade wars with China have been a central cause of market volatility. Then there is the current US government shutdown which is actually a standoff between Republicans and Democrats about the Great Wall of Mexico. Brexit continues to dominate European headlines, because the deadline is the end of March 2019. I saw an article suggesting that around $1 trillion in assets and insurance capital might be relocated to mainland Europe in the event of a hard Brexit. Financial firms are close to just calling it and checking out, because of the uncertainty.
Finally we have the Fed, which was previously committed to multiple interest rate hikes in 2019, but now seem to have cooled down. Now I (Byron here) know that I am talking my own book, because low interest rates are good for markets, but I do feel the Fed has jumped the gun a little with their recent increases. Commodity prices are low thanks to manufacturing efficiencies and the US Dollar is strong. If inflation is not at threatening levels then just let the economy be for the time being. That's my view.
So far this year The JSE All-share is down 1.6%, the S&P 500 is up 2.6%, and the Nasdaq is up 3.63%.
One Thing, from Paul
So it turns out that the best place to put your money in 2018 was cash . For the first time in decades, every major type of investment fared poorly. If your own returns were poor last year, you are not alone. See the chart below, from Bloomberg.
Annus Horribilis chart
Another Thing, from Paul
Felix Salmon at Axios points out that "at the end of December, a huge American consumer brand announced a blockbuster quarter, driven largely by sales in China. Before accounting for currency fluctuations, Nike (NYSE: NKE )'s quarterly sales soared 31% in China, with digital sales in the country growing even more." When Nike stock started trading after the results were announced, its shares were up more than 8.5% from where they had closed the previous day.
Then, "at the beginning of January, a huge American consumer brand announced it was going to have a disappointing quarter, driven largely by sales in China. For the first time this century, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) will see a year-on-year revenue decline in the all-important final quarter of the calendar year." When Apple stock started trading after the results were announced, its shares were down some 8.8% from where they had closed the previous day.
It is interesting to see such different outcomes from companies operating in the same economy. I guess that this is how it goes sometimes? The Chinese market is very large, and very competitive. It is also slowing currently, and there is lots of drama as Trump's trade war creates unpredictable second-order effects.
These companies will make strategic adjustments to gain market share. We advise you to hold tightly onto both of them or buy more .
Signing off
It is great to be back. The team is full of energy and optimistic for a better 2019. The US market is showing signs of recovery. A lower oil price and a stronger Rand is a nice boost for our local consumer. The retailers will soon start releasing updates from the festive period. That should be interesting.
